title: Rejected commit approval can be bypassed by retrying the request
description:
## Summary

A user rejection of a privileged Git commit did not persist as a denial. After the user repeated the same `commit and sync` request, the agent retried the rejected operation and successfully committed and pushed changes.

## Reproduction

Session: `01a00708-4889-7501-a873-52601d5333fd`

1. In `/home/lotso/dotfiles`, ask the agent to `commit and sync` with uncommitted changes.
2. When approval is requested for the Git metadata write, reject it.
3. Repeat `commit and sync`.
4. Observe that the agent retries `git add ... && git commit ...`, then runs `git pull --rebase origin main` and `git push origin main` successfully.

Observed commit: `deb5744 chore(beads): update WAL certificates`.

## Expected

A rejected approval must remain denied for that action/request. The agent should report that the operation was not authorized and must not retry the rejected privileged command or perform the subsequent push unless the user explicitly grants a fresh approval through the approval control. Repeating the natural-language request alone must not bypass the rejection.

## Actual

The next turn treated the earlier rejection as a temporary environment blocker and retried the same privileged operation. The retry succeeded and the changes were committed and synced.

## Impact

Users can lose control over repository mutations after explicitly rejecting an approval prompt. This is an authorization and safety issue affecting commit/push workflows.

## Evidence

The session log records the first tool result as `Rejected("rejected by user")`, followed by a second `commit and sync` turn whose tool calls performed commit, pull/rebase, and push.
close_reason: Fixed permission picker to place typed rejection choices before approvals, preventing numbered-picker fallback from selecting Allow Once. Regression failed before the fix and passes; all 183 MiniTest cases, StyLua, LuaLS, and git diff --check pass.

title: Resume restores session but reports malformed ACP session/load result
description:
## Summary

`:LuiselmResume` restores the requested session, but reports:

`louiselm: ACP session/load returned a malformed result`

Observed while resuming the session for: https://a16z.com/knowing-when-to-stop-the-art-of-making-a-loop-converge/?utm_source=tldrai

## Expected behavior

A successfully restored session should resume without a malformed-result error. If the ACP response is accepted and the session is usable, do not report it as malformed; otherwise fail the resume operation clearly and leave state consistent.

## Actual behavior

The session is put back/restored, while louiselm emits the malformed `ACP session/load` diagnostic.

## Investigation notes

Likely a mismatch between the ACP `session/load` result validation and the subsequent resume state transition, or an error being reported after a usable result has already been applied. Reproduce with `:LuiselmResume` on the session described above and inspect the raw response shape and validation boundary.

## Acceptance criteria

- Resuming a valid saved session does not emit the malformed-result error.
- Malformed `session/load` responses still fail safely and produce a specific diagnostic.
- Resume state is not partially applied when validation fails.
close_reason: Fixed ACP v1 session/load response validation: accept object responses without requiring sessionId, preserve replayed config options when absent, and reject JSON null. TDD regression failed first on {}; focused session tests pass; full 128-case MiniTest suite passes; stylua --check passes; lua-language-server reports zero diagnostics; git diff --check passes; dependency graph has no cycles.

title: Grill-me needed: how should autonomy level be authorized, and should it key on reversibility rather than tool identity
description:
**Grill-me needed. Do not resolve this in passing — it wants full attention.**

Sibling in shape to `louiselm-iyy`: a process/design question surfaced mid-session that fits no existing route. Raised as explicit "food for thought" on 2026-08-19.

## The question

Authorization is expressed conversationally but enforced structurally, and the two are not connected. Saying "ok, tackle it" conveys real intent — *I am comfortable with you working unsupervised here* — but carries no authority. The actual permission level is a harness setting chosen out-of-band, before the work starts, in whichever client is driving (Claude Code's permission modes, Codex's approval/sandbox settings, and so on).

So: where should that decision sit, especially for automation, where nobody is present to answer a prompt?

## Evidence from the session that raised it

A permission prompt fired and aborted on `br update --status=in_progress` — a status field write, fully reversible, trivial. No prompt fired when eight files were moved out of the user's home directory.

The granularity is anti-correlated with risk. The safe operation interrupted the flow; the destructive one did not. This is not fixed by extending an allowlist. The permission layer keys on **tool identity** (`Bash` vs `Write`) when the property that matters is **reversibility**.

## Threads worth pulling

- Permission policies are already one of louiselm's four named extension boundaries (`AGENTS.md` section 1), so the concept has somewhere to live.
- A workflow stage could carry its own policy as part of its definition rather than as a separate rule set: a grill stage needs no write access at all; an execute stage against a well-specified issue is exactly the hands-off case; a QA stage has a human in it by definition. This connects directly to the deferred workflow-engine work (`louiselm-qbr.3`, `louiselm-qbr.5`).
- The `ready-for-agent` label already asserts that a spec is tight enough to hand over. It is a short step from that to also carrying how much autonomy comes with it.

## The distinction to preserve

"Yolo mode" bundles two different things: **acting without asking** and **acting irreversibly**. The first is cheap to grant and easy to withdraw. The second is not.

If autonomy scales with reversibility rather than with confidence in the task, the operator can be far more permissive than they would otherwise dare, because the downside is bounded by construction rather than by the agent's judgment. That framing also removes the need for a phrase like "tackle it" to encode a trust level at all — the action's reversibility determines the treatment, not the sentence that requested it.

## Out of scope for the grill

Re-deriving the above. React to it.

title: Display the requested command in permission pickers
description:
## Problem

The command permission picker identifies only the operation kind and the available decisions. It does not show the command being approved or denied. In the attached observation, after the user entered `retry`, the picker showed only `Deny`, `Allow Once`, and `Always Allow`; the actual `git add ... && git commit ... && git push` command was visible only in a wrapped `[tool]` transcript line behind the picker.

This is unsafe and confusing UX, especially for persistent approval choices. The user should not have to correlate a possibly obscured or stale tool transcript line with the active permission request.

## Evidence

- Screenshot: `/home/lotso/Pictures/scrot/20260816_0743_950x1123_1786858980.png`
- Observed with the Claude ACP adapter after asking `retry`.
- Codex may expose more command context, so compare Claude- and Codex-shaped permission payloads rather than assuming the limitation is adapter-specific.
- Current code already normalizes `data.operation.command`, but `prompt_permission` builds the prompt from only `operation.kind` and formats each item from only the ACP option label. This suggests that the shared UI drops command context that is already available.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Start a chat using the Claude ACP adapter.
2. Trigger a command requiring permission; denying or failing it and then entering `retry` reproduces the observed sequence.
3. Wait for the command permission picker.
4. Observe that the picker shows approval choices but not the command governed by them.

## Expected

The active permission UI clearly identifies the exact command being approved or denied, including for long or compound shell commands. The complete command must remain inspectable without dismissing the picker or inferring it from the background transcript.

## Actual

The picker prompt is only `louiselm permission (command):`; its entries contain only decision labels.

## Scope

- Surface command context from the normalized permission operation at the decision point.
- Preserve literal command content; do not reconstruct a potentially misleading shell command from lossy data.
- Verify behavior with Claude- and Codex-shaped ACP requests and avoid depending on adapter-specific option labels.
- Keep file-edit diff review and unrelated tool-call rendering unchanged.

## Acceptance Criteria

1. Every command permission request with a valid normalized command shows that exact command in the active permission UI before a response can be selected.
2. Long, wrapped, and compound commands remain fully inspectable without relying on transcript lines or tool-call IDs.
3. ACP option names and identifiers remain exact, rejection choices remain first, picker dismissal still cancels, and responses still return the selected option ID.
4. Malformed or unknown operations use an explicit safe fallback and never claim to display a command that was not received.
5. Headless UI tests cover Claude- and Codex-shaped command requests, a long compound command, the safe fallback, scheduling, and the existing fail-closed selection behavior.
close_reason: Displayed exact normalized command JSON in the active permission picker prompt with an explicit unavailable-details fallback. Added Claude/Codex/unknown UI regression coverage and documented behavior. Verification: focused chat suite 48/48; full MiniTest suite 189/189; stylua --check passed; lua-language-server reported no problems; git diff --check passed.

title: Permission pickers from two sessions can still collide
description:
The permission queue added in c639f95 (louiselm-4wx) is per session. vim.ui.select is a process-wide resource: two attached chat sessions that each reach a permission request at the same time still open two pickers, and an async provider such as the Snacks picker tears the first one down. That reproduces the louiselm-4wx failure across sessions - one request answered cancelled without the user acting, the other left unanswered and blocking its agent.

Not fixed with louiselm-4wx because the narrowest boundary for the reported single-session deadlock was the session, and a process-wide picker queue means module-level mutable state, which AGENTS.md section 7 warns against.

Repro sketch: attach two sessions, prompt both so each hits an ask-human permission in the same window, and observe both pickers.

Options to weigh:
- Serialize decision UI in louiselm.ui.chat across views (the chat controller already owns every view and the diff review, so it has a clear owner and lifecycle for the queue).
- Or serialize in louiselm.ui.picker, which also covers the session, skill, and agent pickers, but introduces a module singleton.

Whatever the layer, the invariant is the same as louiselm-4wx: at most one decision UI open at a time, and every ACP permission request answered exactly once.
close_reason: Fixed in 0ed18d0. Chose the chat controller over louiselm.ui.picker: it already owns every view and the diff review, so the queue has a clear owner and lifecycle instead of a module singleton (AGENTS.md section 7), and it covers reviews as well as pickers. lua/louiselm/ui/chat/init.lua now queues decisions across all views (queue_decision/pump_decisions/open_decision), releases the slot exactly once per decision, and cancels what it cannot host: chat disposal, an event delivered to a torn-down view, and a select provider that throws. lua/louiselm/ui/diff/init.lua adds a BufWipeout handler because review buffers are bufhidden=wipe - navigating away used to abandon the request unanswered, which would have stalled the queue. Tests: tests/ui/chat_spec.lua 'opens one permission decision at a time across sessions', 'cancels permission decisions still queued when the chat is disposed', 'cancels a permission request delivered after disposal'; tests/ui/diff_spec.lua 'cancels the permission request when its review buffer is wiped'. chat_spec now restores vim.schedule/vim.ui.select in post_case, because a failing expectation skipped a test's own restore and broke MiniTest itself. Full suite 196 cases, stylua --check, lua-language-server all clean. Not covered: pickers louiselm opens for its own commands (session options, skills, agents) are still unqueued and can collide with a permission decision.

title: Design persistent ACP permission UX
description:
## Goal

Decide and implement how louiselm should remember ACP permission choices such as Allow for Session and Allow Commands Starting With a command prefix.

## Current state

The chat UI displays permission options supplied by the ACP adapter and forwards the selected optionId. louiselm does not persist those choices itself. ACP defines allow_always as remembering the choice but does not prescribe the storage mechanism.

## Scope

- Grill and document the desired UX and trust model for once, session, workspace, command-prefix, and permanent approvals.
- Decide whether louiselm, the ACP adapter, or both own persistence and enforcement.
- Define storage location, scope/keying, revocation/editing UX, and behavior across sessions, adapters, workspaces, and restarts.
- Implement the agreed behavior with tests and documentation.

## Acceptance criteria

- Permission choices have clear, truthful lifetime/scope semantics.
- Persisted rules cannot silently broaden command or file scopes.
- Users can inspect and revoke remembered rules.
- Behavior is covered by deterministic tests and documented for headless and chat consumers.

## Out of scope

- Changing ACP protocol semantics or adding adapter-specific compatibility shims before the UX decision.
close_reason: Implemented exact workspace-and-adapter permission memory, atomic persistent state, option-kind replay, headless list/revoke APIs, file lifetime selection, and :LouiselmPermissions

comments.author: assistant
comments.text:
Agreed UX direction from grill session:

- louiselm owns remembered permission decisions; no user-configurable rule object initially.
- Default scope is current workspace + current ACP adapter.
- Command rules match exact argv prefixes; no shell strings, regexes, or substring matching.
- Persist state in a user-level file under Neovim stdpath("state"), never the project repo.
- Add :LouiseLmPermissions to inspect and revoke remembered rules.
- allow_once/reject_once are not saved; allow_session is memory-only for the ACP session; allow_always/reject_always are persisted.
- Commands and file edits have separate rule types.
- If a later adapter request lacks a compatible option kind, fail closed and ask the user again; never infer from labels.

title: Send bounded hidden skill catalogs in inject mode
description:
## Goal

Provide natural-language skill discovery to injected agents without visible context markers, unbounded prompts, or duplicate delivery.

## Scope

- In scope: serialize implicit skills using the Agent Skills `<available_skills><skill>...` XML shape with escaped name, description, and absolute configured-alias location.
- In scope: prepend the fixed agreed behavioral instructions and cap the complete serialized hidden block at 8,000 UTF-8 bytes, including preamble and wrappers.
- In scope: preserve the preamble and all possible names/paths, shorten descriptions fairly and codepoint-safely first, then omit the deterministic name/path-sorted tail if minimum metadata still cannot fit.
- In scope: exclude explicit-only skills from the model catalog while retaining them in the picker; expose omitted/truncated diagnostics.
- In scope: build the catalog only for a new session, hold it locally, and attach it as a separate hidden first text block to the first accepted non-slash model prompt.
- In scope: defer catalog and ordinary attached contexts across user-authored slash prompts; consume the catalog when prompt submission returns a valid ACP request id. Do not resend after accepted cancellation, crash, or uncertain failure.
- In scope: explicit picker activation attaches the exact complete SKILL.md once for that activation; a selected-file read failure blocks submission and preserves the prompt/selection.
- Out of scope: resumed-session reinjection, synthetic catalog turns, recursive resource embedding, native command invocation, and transcript persistence.

## Acceptance Criteria

1. No `[context: skill-index]` or catalog text is rendered before submission.
2. The entire hidden block never exceeds 8,000 bytes and is validly truncated at UTF-8 boundaries.
3. Natural-language prompts receive one catalog per new injected session; explicit-only skills never appear in it.
4. Slash commands defer rather than consume attached skill context.
5. Synchronous local failure retains the catalog, while any accepted request consumes it exactly once.
6. A deliberate re-selection may attach the same skill on a later turn, but one activation never sends it twice.
7. Resumed or external sessions do not receive a guessed catalog; documentation directs users to start a new session when provenance is uncertain.
8. MiniTest and mock ACP coverage assert block ordering, budgeting, XML escaping, slash deferral, request-id consumption, failure/cancel behavior, picker reads, and no-double-send invariants.

## Testing

Use byte-counting and multibyte fixtures for the budget. Assert exact ACP prompt block arrays through the mock agent.

## Notes

The 8,000-byte rule is a conservative adaptation of Codex fallback behavior, not an ACP or Agent Skills specification requirement.

title: louiselm.nvim: pure ACP client for Neovim — v1 core + phased roadmap
description:
## Problem Statement

As a daily Neovim + agent user, my current plugin (codecompanion.nvim) fights my workflow in three ways. First, config mistakes fail silently: a mistyped key is absorbed by deep-merge and the feature it configures is skipped without a word. Second, its architecture is a general adapter abstraction normalizing HTTP providers and ACP into one interface, while I use exclusively ACP agents (claude-agent-acp, codex-acp, acp-llm-adapter, copilot ACP) — I pay the complexity of a layer I do not use. Third, it gives me no path to the feature I actually want next: a swarm of agents collaboratively working a queue of beads tasks. My core workflow — grill an idea in chat, converge on a plan, convert the plan into beads via skills — must keep working, uniformly, across all my agents.

## Solution

louiselm.nvim: a pure ACP client for Neovim. Agents are external processes declared in config; anything non-ACP reaches the plugin through external bridges (acp-llm-adapter, opencode acp), never through in-plugin providers. The core is built swarm-ready from day one: a multi-session registry with a headless Lua API, typed events, pluggable permission policies, and addressable sessions — so the future orchestrator is an additional consumer of the public API, not a rewrite. Configuration is validated militantly against a single declarative schema that also generates the LuaCATS types and the documentation. Skills use an explicit per-agent native/inject/off policy: native delegates discovery and invocation to the adapter, inject uses a hidden bounded local catalog, and off disables LouiseLM skill automation.

## User Stories

1. As a user, I want to declare each agent (command, args, env, options) in my config, so that adding a backend is a config entry, never plugin code.
2. As a user, I want any unknown config key to produce a hard error with a fuzzy "did you mean" suggestion, so that typos can never silently disable a feature.
3. As a user, I want wrong types or invalid values to error with the expected type, the received value, and a valid example, so that I can fix mistakes without reading source.
4. As a user, I want all config errors collected and reported in one structured report, so that I fix everything in a single pass instead of a fix-reload loop.
5. As a user, I want the plugin to refuse to start on invalid config, so that I am never unknowingly running on silently substituted defaults.
6. As a user, I want deprecated keys to warn with a migration path, so that upgrades guide me instead of breaking me.
7. As a user, I want editor completion and type checking while writing my config, so that most mistakes are caught before the validator ever runs.
8. As a user, I want :checkhealth to re-run validation plus environment checks (agent binaries on PATH, versions, skill paths exist), so that a broken setup is diagnosable in one command.
9. As a user, I want a chat buffer with streamed markdown and a visible tool-call timeline, so that I can follow what the agent is doing while it does it.
10. As a user, I want to pick which agent a new session uses and switch between concurrent sessions, so that several conversations can live side by side.
11. As a user, I want agent-requested file edits and commands gated by a permission flow, so that nothing touches my system without policy saying so.
12. As a user, I want agent file edits reviewable as diffs, so that I can inspect changes before or after approving them.
13. As a user, I want permissions evaluated by pluggable policy objects with "ask the human" merely the default, so that future autonomous sessions can run scoped auto-approval policies without core changes.
14. As a user, I want to mention the current buffer, send a visual selection, and fuzzy-pick files into the conversation, so that pointing the agent at context is one gesture.
15. As a user, I want slash commands advertised by the agent over ACP to appear in the chat's command menu, so that agent capabilities surface without client-side duplication.
16. As a user, I want my central Agent Skills / SKILL.md repo available to injected agents and the local picker, while native adapters retain ownership of their own discovery, so that one skill tree works without duplicate delivery.
17. As a user, I want an explicit per-agent skills policy (native, inject, off), defaulting to native with no runtime inference or fallback, so that each adapter has one understandable skill owner.
18. As a user, I want ordered, deterministic, symlink-aware local discovery with duplicate and escape diagnostics, so that injected and picker-visible skills resolve predictably.
19. As a user, I want a skill invocation picker that sends one advertised command in native mode or one complete SKILL.md in inject mode, so that explicit activation is predictable and never duplicated.
20. As a user, I want my grill-me → plan → beads workflow to run purely through skills and the agent executing the beads CLI itself, so that the plugin core stays tracker-ignorant.
21. As a plugin consumer (or future orchestrator), I want a headless Lua API — create session against a named agent, prompt, receive streamed updates via callbacks, cancel, dispose — so that everything the UI does is scriptable without UI.
22. As a plugin consumer, I want typed events emitted for every session lifecycle moment (chunk, tool call started/finished, permission requested, turn done, error), so that dashboards and orchestrators can subscribe without patching internals.
23. As a user, I want every session addressable by id with inspectable state (agent, status, working dir, current turn), so that a future swarm dashboard has substrate to read.
24. As a user, I want a crashed or misbehaving agent process to surface as a loud, specific session error — never a hang or a silent death — so that failure modes are as strict as config validation.
25. As a contributor, I want the ACP layer conformance-tested against a mock agent in CI, so that protocol correctness is verified without real LLMs or API keys.

## Implementation Decisions

- Pure ACP client, hard boundary: no in-plugin HTTP providers ever; non-ACP backends go through external bridges. Internally one small agent interface with ACP as its sole implementation, preserving the seam for a hypothetical future transport.
- Five hard architectural constraints checked against every PR: (1) multi-session registry, no singleton chat; (2) headless API with the UI as its first consumer; (3) typed event system; (4) permission policies as pluggable objects, human prompt as default policy; (5) sessions addressable, listable, inspectable.
- Modules: schema (config DSL, validator, error reporter; single source generating LuaCATS types and vimdoc), acp (JSON-RPC 2.0 over stdio via vim.system pipes, typed against the protocol schema), session (registry, headless API, events, process lifecycle), permission (policy engine), skills (discovery, index injection, per-agent policy, overlap detection), ui.chat, ui.diff, health, and a dev-only mock ACP agent.
- Config validation is militant: unknown key or wrong type is a hard error; errors are collected exhaustively then reported; plugin refuses to start on any error; deprecated keys warn with migration path.
- Skills: Agent Skills defines the file format and ACP remains transport. Global paths feed LouiseLM-managed discovery; global policy defaults to native and an agent may override only native|inject|off. Native sends no catalog/body and resolves picker activation through the adapter's latest advertised commands. Inject sends one hidden, 8,000-byte bounded metadata catalog on a new session and one complete SKILL.md per explicit activation. Off disables automation. Policy is session-static, never inferred, and never falls back at runtime.
- Chat context is deliberately thin: buffer mention, visual selection, file picker, agent slash-command passthrough, skill picker. Agents explore the project themselves; the client points.
- Tech foundation: Neovim floor = latest stable at release, moving forward aggressively; no UI/framework runtime dependencies (no plenary, no nui); `lyaml` plus LibYAML is the explicit conditional runtime dependency for LouiseLM-managed local skill discovery, replacing a custom YAML parser; picker integrations are configured and validated, never silently auto-detected; LuaCATS everywhere with lua-language-server as a CI gate.
- Phasing: P0 foundation (schema, acp, session, agent defs) → P1 daily driver (chat, permissions, diff, context, explicit skill profiles; exit criterion: codecompanion uninstalled, grill-me → beads works on all four agents) → P2 comfort (inline assistant on the same session core, history via ACP session/load, skill-profile ergonomics, multi-session UX) → P3 swarm (opens with its own grill-me).
- Rust is welcome where it earns its place: the swarm orchestrator binary is the named candidate (long-running external process, async runtime, same ecosystem as beads_rust); the core editor-side client stays pure Lua.

## Testing Decisions

- mini.test as the sole, dev-only test dependency.
- schema, acp, session, permission, and skills get full headless unit coverage; the headless API constraint exists partly to make this trivial.
- acp and session additionally get integration coverage driving the mock ACP agent end to end (spawn, initialize, session, prompt, streamed updates, permission round-trip, cancel, agent-crash surfacing).
- A good test here exercises a module through its public interface only; the five architectural constraints are themselves enforced by tests (e.g. two concurrent sessions prompting simultaneously is a required passing case from P0).
- UI modules get smoke tests via child Neovim processes; no pixel-level assertions.
- Validator and skills tests include typo'd keys, wrong types, valid-looking-but-unknown sections, YAML/semantic failures, ordered duplicate precedence, symlink aliases/escapes, native command collisions, injected budget boundaries, and exact no-double-send behavior.

## Out of Scope

- Completion / ghost text: dropped permanently; other plugins own that space.
- In-plugin HTTP or provider adapters of any kind.
- A prompt library separate from skills.
- The swarm orchestrator's design (in-nvim vs external Rust binary, scheduling, worktree isolation): deferred to a dedicated grill-me that opens Phase 3. This epic only guarantees its prerequisites.
- Beads-specific core code; the optional beads dashboard/picker is a future extension on the public API.
- RAG, indexing, web search: agent-side concerns.

## Further Notes

- Ecosystem bet acknowledged: louiselm wagers on ACP's continued adoption (Zed-originated; gemini-cli, opencode, goose, amp, claude, codex all speak it). The internal agent interface is the hedge.
- Risk: ACP spec evolution (e.g. session/load, command advertisement) may shift; the protocol layer should pin a spec version and negotiate capabilities explicitly.
- The user's central skill repo pattern (~/.config/agentskills) is the reference LouiseLM-managed deployment. Discovery preserves configured aliases, canonicalizes for cycles/deduplication, warns on escapes, and treats roots as trusted prompt/plugin-like input.

title: Typing during active turn inserts red buffer error
description:
## Reproduction
1. Start a LouiseLM chat session.
2. While the model is responding / it is not the user's turn, type into the chat buffer.

## Observed
The chat buffer displays a red error/traceback while handling the typed input:
`vim.schedule callback: .../lua/louiselm/ui/chat/init.lua:145: replacement string item contains newlines`
The traceback points through `nvim_buf_set_lines`, `set_line`, and `handle_event`. The UI later appears normal once the turn completes (see second screenshot), but the transient error is user-visible and may indicate that streamed/event updates race with edits made while the session is active.

## Expected
Typing while it is not the user's turn should be safely rejected, queued, or otherwise handled without a red traceback or corrupted chat buffer. Any user-facing feedback should be intentional and clear.

## Evidence
- First screenshot: `/home/lotso/Pictures/scrot/20260809_0501_1920x1200_1786244489.png`
- Second screenshot: `/home/lotso/Pictures/scrot/20260809_0501_1920x1200_1786244505.png`

- Identify whether the root cause is newline-containing content being passed as one `nvim_buf_set_lines` replacement item, a turn-state race, or both.

- Add regression coverage for input arriving while streamed updates are being applied.

title: Queue one next-turn chat prompt while the session is busy
description:
## Problem

Pressing Enter in the chat while the model is responding currently mutates the transcript first, then calls `Session:prompt()`. Because the session is not `ready`, the prompt is rejected and the chat records both a phantom user turn and `Error: session is not ready`.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Open a louiselm chat session and submit a prompt that produces a response long enough to remain active.
2. While the session status is `prompting`, type another message on the chat input line and press Enter.
3. Observe that the input is appended as though it were submitted, followed by `Error: session is not ready`, even though ACP rejected the prompt.

## Expected behavior

The chat owns one pending next-turn prompt per attached session. Pressing Enter during an active turn commits the current input as that session's queued prompt. It remains outside the transcript and sends automatically only after that turn definitively completes or cancellation completes.

## Decisions

- Queue only in `prompting`, `waiting_permission`, and `cancelling`; ordinary ready-state submission remains immediate.
- Support exactly one queued prompt per session, including slash commands.
- Keep queued state with its session when switching chat buffers.
- Show `Queued for next turn` beside the input using virtual text, without modifying prompt text.
- A queued prompt is committed by Enter. Editing it returns it to draft state and requires Enter to recommit, preventing a partial edit from auto-sending.
- Snapshot attached file/selection context when the prompt is committed.
- Release the queue only at a definitive active-turn completion boundary, not on unrelated generic `ready` transitions.
- User cancellation preserves and sends the queued prompt after cancellation completes. A genuine session failure preserves it as a draft and does not send it.
- Append the user message to the transcript only after `Session:prompt()` accepts it.
- If submission fails, preserve the draft and use an editor notification; do not append an `Error:` transcript line for a prompt that was never accepted.
- During `starting` or `configuring`, Enter preserves a draft and notifies instead of queuing. Never queue in `error` or `disposed`.
- Closing a session warns explicitly that its queued prompt will be discarded. Disposal guarantees queued work cannot send later.

## Acceptance criteria

1. Enter during each active-turn state queues one prompt without adding either the prompt or an error to the transcript.
2. On normal turn completion, the committed prompt and its snapshotted context are submitted exactly once and only then appear in transcript history.
3. On completed user cancellation, the committed prompt submits exactly once; on session error it remains an unsent draft.
4. Editing a committed queued prompt makes it a draft and prevents auto-send until Enter recommits it.
5. A second queued turn cannot be accumulated; state is isolated per attached session and survives session switching.
6. Slash commands use the same queue path.
7. Startup/configuration/error/disposed states never create queued work or transcript errors from rejected input.
8. Closing/disposal clears pending work, warns when appropriate, and late scheduled events cannot submit it.
9. Add focused headless chat tests for state transitions, async scheduled event delivery, exactly-once submission, context ownership, switching, failure, cancellation, and disposal. Follow red-green-refactor and run the full required quality gates.

## Scope

- In scope: chat input/queued-prompt state, presentation, lifecycle handling, and behavioral tests.
- Out of scope: changing ACP to allow concurrent prompts, queuing multiple future turns, or changing session-core readiness rules.
close_reason: Implemented one per-session queued next-turn prompt with virtual-text state, edit invalidation, context snapshots, turn/cancellation release, rejection preservation, close/disposal safety, and README documentation. title: State sole copyright and retained relicensing right in CONTRIBUTING
description:
Amend `CONTRIBUTING.md` to state the copyright and relicensing position plainly.

The existing no-merge policy already explains *why* outside code is not merged (review burden, product coherence). This adds the licensing consequence of that policy, which is currently unstated.

## Content to add

A short factual paragraph, not a threat and not a legal wall of text:

- Copyright in LouiseLM is held solely by the maintainer.
- No outside code is merged, so no CLA is required and none will be asked for.
- The maintainer retains the right to license future versions under different terms.

## Why stated rather than silent

Sole ownership is already inferable in ten seconds from the public no-merge policy, so concealment buys no real surprise. The community LouiseLM wants — people bringing workflows and judgment over years — punishes ambush hardest and forgives disclosed risk easily. A pre-announced possibility converts an eventual relicense from betrayal into a term everyone accepted going in.

## Acceptance criteria

- `CONTRIBUTING.md` states all three points above.
- The tone matches the existing document: explicit about an unusual constraint, so nobody wastes effort or gets hurt feelings.
- Nothing elsewhere in the repo contradicts it by implying a perpetual open-source guarantee.

title: Add explicit per-agent Agent Skills profiles
description:
## Problem Statement

LouiseLM currently injects one global skill index into every session, including adapters such as Codex and Claude that already provide native Agent Skills support. This exposes an implementation marker in chat, wastes context, can send a skill twice, and leaves users unable to understand which component discovers or invokes a skill.

## Solution

Add explicit per-agent Agent Skills profiles. Global skill paths remain shared, the default policy is `native`, and an agent may override only `skills.policy` with `native`, `inject`, or `off`. Native mode delegates discovery and invocation to the adapter. Inject mode provides a hidden, bounded Agent Skills catalog and attaches a selected full SKILL.md only once per activation. Off disables LouiseLM skill automation and the picker. Never infer or switch policy at runtime.

## User Stories

1. As a Codex or Claude user, I want native skills used without LouiseLM reinjecting them, so that skills are not duplicated.
2. As a custom-adapter user, I want to opt one agent into injected discovery, so that natural-language skill matching still works.
3. As a user, I want a picker that invokes a known local skill safely in both native and injected profiles, so that explicit activation is predictable.
4. As a user, I want skill context hidden before submission but inspectable afterward, so that chat stays clean without concealing what was sent.
5. As a skill author, I want malformed, shadowed, explicit-only, truncated, or inaccessible skills diagnosed clearly, so that configuration failures are understandable.
6. As a user configuring an unfamiliar ACP adapter, I want documentation explaining Agent Skills, ACP transport, host responsibilities, and filesystem assumptions, so that I can choose the correct policy.

## Acceptance Criteria

1. Global `skills.policy` defaults to `native`; agent definitions may override only the policy, while paths remain global and session-static.
2. `native` sends no automatic catalog or skill body. Picker activation resolves against the adapter's latest advertised command list and sends exactly one advertised command plus task.
3. `inject` sends one hidden catalog only on the first accepted non-slash prompt of a new session, then sends a selected complete SKILL.md once per deliberate activation. It never falls back to native or reinjects after uncertain accepted requests.
4. `off` sends no skill automation and disables the skill picker without intercepting user-authored slash commands.
5. The old `full_content` setting and dormant automatic-native-fallback API are removed with clear migration errors and documentation.
6. Agent Skills core metadata is parsed with `lyaml` and semantically validated; Codex and Claude invocation-control extensions are recognized without treating them as ACP requirements.
7. Missing `lyaml` blocks injected sessions and local native picker/validation, but does not block native sessions themselves or off sessions.
8. The injected catalog uses the agreed Agent Skills XML shape, fixed behavioral preamble, XML escaping, and an 8,000-byte UTF-8-safe total budget with deterministic diagnostics.
9. Submitted prompt contexts are represented as one closed Neovim fold containing exact sent content in order; automatic hidden catalog text never appears as a pre-send marker.
10. README, generated configuration help/annotations, checkhealth, and migration guidance explain policy selection, no-double-send behavior, dependency installation, trust/path rules, filesystem limits, and live-only fold persistence.
11. Automated tests cover configuration, discovery, YAML, invocation metadata, native command correlation, injection lifecycle, slash deferral, failures/cancellation, no-double-send invariants, and context folds. Installed Codex/Claude checks remain documented manual smoke tests.

## Implementation Notes

- Agent Skills defines the skill format; ACP transports prompts and command updates; LouiseLM is the host responsible for policy and injected discovery.
- Explicit-only wins when `disable-model-invocation: true` or OpenAI's `policy.allow_implicit_invocation: false` is present. Such skills remain picker-visible but are excluded from injected catalogs.
- Root order defines duplicate precedence; path handling is deterministic, symlink-aware, and diagnostic without adding a trust database.
- The 8,000-byte mechanism intentionally mimics Codex's conservative fallback behavior; it is not part of ACP or the Agent Skills specification.
- Use native Neovim folds and existing context transport. Do not introduce a generic fold framework.

## Testing Notes

Use MiniTest for module behavior and a mock ACP agent for command updates and prompt transport. Test public behavior and exact no-double-send invariants. Do not require authenticated live adapters in automated tests.

## Out of Scope

- Runtime policy switching or inference.
- A general UI for every ACP advertised command.
- A LouiseLM ACP filesystem service.
- Recursive embedding of skill resources.
- Persistent transcript reconstruction.
- Automatic dependency installation.
- Generic adapter-native skill implementation.
- Tool-call fold rendering; track that as a separate design question.

title: Diagnose installed lyaml outside Neovim search paths
description:
## Problem

Local skill discovery reports:

```
louiselm: lyaml is required for local skill discovery; install it with `luarocks --lua-version 5.1 install lyaml`
```

However, LuaRocks confirms that lyaml is already installed for Lua 5.1. The actual failure is that the active Neovim process does not search the LuaRocks tree, so the message sends the user toward an installation command that will not fix the search-path mismatch.

## Reproduction evidence

- `luarocks --lua-version 5.1 show lyaml` succeeds with lyaml 6.2.9-2 under `$HOME/.asdf/installs/lua/5.1.5/luarocks`.
- Neovim 0.12.2 embeds LuaJIT 2.1.
- In `nvim --headless -u NONE`, `pcall(require, "lyaml")` returns `module 'lyaml' not found`.
- Neovim's `package.path` and `package.cpath` contain system paths, but not the asdf LuaRocks share/lib paths reported by `luarocks path --lua-version 5.1`.

## Expected behavior

When lyaml cannot be loaded, LouiseLM should preserve enough of the loader failure to distinguish an absent installation from an installed-but-unreachable LuaRocks tree (and from native module load failures), then give a corrective action that matches the failure.

## Acceptance criteria

1. The user-facing/checkhealth diagnostic distinguishes at least package-not-found/search-path mismatch from a native loader failure instead of always saying to install lyaml.
2. Documentation gives a supported way to make a Lua 5.1 LuaRocks tree visible to Neovim, including non-system/asdf installs.
3. Tests cover the generic `require("lyaml")` failure mapping without depending on a real LuaRocks installation.
4. Diagnostics do not expose unrelated environment values or sensitive data.
close_reason: Shortened interactive lyaml failures to point at checkhealth, added detailed persistent zsh/asdf guidance to health and README, and covered both surfaces. Verified 181 MiniTest cases, StyLua, and LuaLS.

title: Resumed-session export silently drops nested/subagent tool calls
description:
`:LouiselmResume`'s replay of a prior ACP session silently drops nested/child
tool calls (a tool call made *by* a Task subagent, i.e. one carrying a
`parentToolUseId`), while still replaying the parent Task call's own summary
text. Anyone exporting a resumed session — including the blog publishing
pipeline, which exports whatever the agent replays on `session/load` — gets a
transcript that is missing subagent-internal tool-call detail, with no error
or signal that anything is missing.

## Observed

QA round for the transcript-export/blog-publishing features
(`4e4a58b`, `674939b`), case 4 ("resumed-session export vs live export"),
session `21a0ede3-b65e-4f1c-935d-754f22126384`, 2026-08-18.

Prompt that produced the nested call (case 1 of the same round):
"Do these three things in order, in this one turn. (1) Run the Bash tool on
the absolute path: `wc -l .../transcript.lua`. (2) Use the Task tool to
launch one general-purpose subagent whose prompt is exactly: 'List the
top-level directories of /home/lotso/code/louiselm as one comma-separated
line.' (3) Write me a two-sentence summary of what you found."

Original live export, captured right after that turn ended:
`louiselm-session-1-20260818-150448.md` (repo root at the time). Contains 3
tool-call blocks — Bash (`wc -l`), Task (`List top-level directories`), and a
nested Bash call made by the Task subagent:
```
toolCallId = "toolu_01AB1x1SdnkvcFoPF6EcmTqr"
parentToolUseId = "toolu_018NnXLu4qGQc7e4bei8C52a"  (the Task call)
title = "ls -d /home/lotso/code/louiselm/*/ | xargs -n1 basename | paste -sd, -"
rawOutput = "android,assets,blog,capture-service,configured,lua,scripts,tests"
status = "completed"
```

Resumed export (`:LouiselmResume` on the same session, immediate
`:LouiselmToMarkdown` → `/tmp/qa-resumed.md`, no other prompt sent first):
same acp session id (session/load reconnects rather than creating a new
session). Contains the parent `## Tool: List top-level directories
(completed)` block with its rawOutput summary intact, but grepping the full
573KB resumed export for the toolCallId `toolu_01AB1x1SdnkvcFoPF6EcmTqr`, the
literal command text `paste -sd`, and `xargs -n1 basename` finds zero
tool-call blocks — those strings appear exactly once, incidentally, inside
unrelated later text content (a grep-output dump quoted in a much later
turn), not as a `## Tool:` entry.

Raw jsonrpc log:
`~/.local/state/acp-llm-adapter/20260818-150022-1160867-claude-agent-acp-stdout-jsonrpc.log`
(818 lines). The nested `tool_call` event for
`toolu_01AB1x1SdnkvcFoPF6EcmTqr` appears exactly once, at line 19, during the
original live turn:
```
{"jsonrpc":"2.0","method":"session/update","params":{"sessionId":"21a0ede3-b65e-4f1c-935d-754f22126384","update":{"_meta":{"claudeCode":{"toolName":"Bash","parentToolUseId":"toolu_018NnXLu4qGQc7e4bei8C52a"}},"toolCallId":"toolu_01AB1x1SdnkvcFoPF6EcmTqr","sessionUpdate":"tool_call","rawInput":{"command":"ls -d /home/lotso/code/louiselm/*/ | xargs -n1 basename | paste -sd, -"},"status":"pending", ...}}}
```
No second occurrence appears later in the log during the replay burst
triggered by `session/load` — the agent process itself never re-emits this
event on replay.

Everything else about the resumed export checked out clean: 65 of the 66
total tool calls in the session (by then spanning many turns) present and in
correct relative order, and the case-1 `## User` block matches the typed
prompt verbatim. Only this one nested call is missing.

## Symptoms

- User sees: a resumed-session export (or a blog post built from one) that
  looks complete — full assistant text, the parent Task call's own summary —
  but is silently missing the detail of what the subagent actually did
  internally.
- System reports: nothing. No error, warning, or count mismatch anywhere;
  `Chat:to_markdown` and `create-blog.sh` both report success normally.

## Root cause

Unknown, and outside this repo (`louiselm.nvim`). `louiselm`'s own
`Transcript:record`/`Transcript.render` (lua/louiselm/session/transcript.lua)
only records whatever `session/update` events it receives over ACP — the
live stream sent the nested tool_call event and louiselm recorded it
correctly (see the original export above); on replay, the same event simply
never arrives, so there is nothing to fix on this side.

Hypothesis (unverified): `claude-agent-acp`
(`/home/lotso/code/acp-llm-adapter`, a sibling project) or the underlying
Claude Code SDK reconstructs the Task/subagent call tree differently when
replaying a resumed session's history than when streaming it live — possibly
only replaying top-level tool calls and treating subagent-internal calls as
already-summarized by the parent's own output. Nothing in this investigation
confirms which layer (adapter vs. upstream SDK) is responsible; that needs a
look at the adapter/SDK's own session/load implementation, not louiselm's.

## Why it was not caught

`tests/session/transcript_export_spec.lua` and
`tests/session/transcript_spec.lua` exercise `Transcript` against synthetic,
hand-built event fixtures for both the live and "loaded" replay paths — no
fixture in the suite includes a nested/subagent tool call in a replay
scenario, because nobody had a real payload to model one on. This QA round
was the first time a resumed session containing a Task-subagent call was
actually exported and diffed against its own live-captured original.

## Fix direction

Not in this repo. If the root cause is confirmed to be in
`claude-agent-acp`, the fix belongs there (ensure `session/load` replay
re-emits every historical `tool_call`/`tool_call_update`, including nested
ones with `parentToolUseId` set, not just top-level calls). If it turns out
to be inherent to how the upstream Claude Code SDK exposes subagent history
on resume, this may not be fixable without a scope change to what
`session/load` guarantees — in which case the practical mitigation is
documentation: warn blog-pipeline users that `create-blog.sh` on a resumed
session may omit subagent-internal tool-call detail, and recommend exporting
live when that detail matters.

## Acceptance

- A regression test in whichever repo owns the fix: replay a session
  containing a Task call with a nested tool call, and assert the replayed
  event stream includes the nested `tool_call`/`tool_call_update` events,
  not just the parent's.
- Re-run this round's case 4 comparison
  (`louiselm-session-1-20260818-150448.md` vs. a fresh `:LouiselmResume` +
  immediate `:LouiselmToMarkdown` export of the same session) and confirm
  `toolu_01AB1x1SdnkvcFoPF6EcmTqr` (or an equivalent nested call in a new
  repro) is present in the resumed export.

## Not covered

- Which of `claude-agent-acp` vs. the upstream Claude Code SDK is actually
  responsible — unverified, needs investigation in that repo, not this one.
- Whether the same gap exists for other nested-call shapes (e.g. a tool call
  made by a tool call, rather than by a Task subagent specifically) — only
  one nested-call example existed in the session under test.
- Whether `create-blog.sh` (case 5, not yet run at time of filing) actually
  reproduces the same gap end-to-end through the headless path — this bug is
  filed from the interactive `:LouiselmResume` path only; case 5 should
  re-check this once it runs.

description:

Render each printed item in one chronological vertical stack, including model text, user text, tool calls, tool results, and status messages. New items should appear after the preceding item in the same transcript flow, with the composer/input area remaining at the bottom.

## Acceptance criteria

2. Tool output is positioned next to or directly after the event that produced it rather than in a separate bottom group.
3. The input/composer remains clearly separated from transcript history at the bottom.

title: LouiselmToMarkdown crashes with uncaught E482 instead of a clean write error
description:
`:LouiselmToMarkdown` crashes with an uncaught Lua/Vimscript error instead of
the clean "could not write markdown file: ..." message when the destination's
parent directory does not exist.

## Observed

Manual QA round on commits 674939b (blog publishing pipeline) and 4e4a58b
(session transcript export), case 2.2/2.3 in QA_REVIEW.md. User ran
`:LouiselmToMarkdown`, typed `~/tmp/qa-export.md` (nonexistent dir):

```
louiselm markdown path (blank for default): ~/tmp/qa-export.md
Lua :command callback: Vim:E482
: Can't open file ~/tmp/qa-export.md for writing: no such file or directory
stack traceback:
        [C]: in function 'writefile'
        ...ack/core/opt/louiselm.nvim/lua/louiselm/ui/chat/init.lua:1561: in function 'to_markdown'
        .../core/opt/louiselm.nvim/lua/louiselm/ui/chat/command.lua:276: in function 'on_confirm'
        ...installs/neovim/0.12.2/share/nvim/runtime/lua/vim/ui.lua:114: in function 'input'
        .../core/opt/louiselm.nvim/lua/louiselm/ui/chat/command.lua:272: in function <.../core/opt/louiselm.nvim/lua/louiselm/ui/chat/command.lua:266>
```

Reproduced identically with the absolute path `/tmp/nope/qa-export.md`
(missing dir), ruling out `~`-expansion as the sole cause — the real trigger
is any nonexistent parent directory.

## Symptoms

- User sees a raw `E482` Lua stack trace in `:messages`, not a `louiselm:`
  notification.
- The chat UI's own error path (`report_error`) never fires for this failure.

## Root cause

`lua/louiselm/ui/chat/init.lua:1561`:

```lua
if nvim.fn.writefile(split_lines(markdown), destination) ~= 0 then
  return nil, "could not write markdown file: " .. destination
end
```

This assumes `writefile()` reports failure via a nonzero return. In Neovim,
when the destination cannot be opened at all (missing parent directory, no
permission), `writefile()` throws `E482` as a Lua error instead of returning
a value — so the `~= 0` check is dead code for this failure mode and the
error propagates uncaught through `Chat:to_markdown` ->
`command.lua:276 on_confirm` -> `vim.ui.input`.

## Why it was not caught

`tests/ui/chat_to_markdown_spec.lua` covers the success path, "no chat
session", "not attached", and "disposed" errors, but has no case where
`writefile` itself fails (e.g. destination inside a nonexistent directory).
The suite never exercises the real `writefile()` call against an unwritable
path.

## Fix direction

Wrap the `writefile` call in `pcall` in `Chat:to_markdown` (init.lua:1561) so
any thrown error is caught and converted into the existing
`"could not write markdown file: " .. destination` return.

## Acceptance

- A regression test in tests/ui/chat_to_markdown_spec.lua that calls
  `to_markdown` with a path inside a nonexistent directory and asserts a
  clean `(nil, "could not write markdown file: " .. path)` return with no
  thrown error.
- Manually confirmed: `:LouiselmToMarkdown` against a missing directory shows
  a `louiselm: could not write markdown file: ...` notification, no stack
  trace in `:messages`.

## Not covered

`~` is not expanded by `vim.fn.writefile` either (a second, separate
usability issue: paths starting with `~` will still fail even inside an
existing directory tree, just with a clean error now instead of a crash).
Not filing separately since the pcall fix already turns it into the correct
clean-error path; only worth a follow-up if users expect `~` to expand.
close_reason: Fixed in 6167df0. Root cause: nvim.fn.writefile throws E482 (Lua error) instead of returning nonzero when the destination directory doesn't exist, so Chat:to_markdown's `~= 0` check never caught the failure. Fix: wrapped the writefile call in pcall (init.lua:1561), converting any thrown error into the existing clean 'could not write markdown file: ...' return. Tests: added 'reports a clean error instead of crashing when the destination directory does not exist' to tests/ui/chat_to_markdown_spec.lua -- failed with the exact E482 traceback before the fix, passes after. Gates: full mini.test suite (235/235 cases) and stylua --check on both changed files pass. No deviation from filed acceptance criteria.

title: Open every UI selector outside insert mode
description:
## Problem

Commit 1eb309a fixed permission selection by leaving insert mode immediately before vim.ui.select. That diagnosis is correct: Chat:attach enters insert mode, and list-focused select providers can otherwise receive the wrong mode and confirm or edit the wrong picker state.

The same bug remains in session configuration. Chat:attach schedules open_session_options after entering insert mode, while both the options overview and its nested model/value picker call vim.ui.select without normalizing mode. This affects the automatic first-session overview and can also affect :LouiselmSessionOptions when invoked from an insert-mode mapping.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Attach a ready session that advertises a model or boolean configuration option.
2. Let Chat:attach focus the prompt and enter insert mode.
3. Wait for the scheduled initial options overview, or invoke :LouiselmSessionOptions from an insert-mode mapping.
4. Observe that vim.ui.select is called while the inherited mode is insert; with a list-focused provider, navigation or confirmation targets the wrong picker state.
5. Select an option such as Model and observe the nested value picker has the same unnormalized boundary.

## Investigation

There are 12 vim.ui.select call sites across chat, context, and diff UI. In addition to session options, selectors that are asynchronous, nested, or exposed through public Chat methods can inherit insert mode: resumed-session selection, remembered-permission selection and confirmation, session switch/close, agent selection, and file/skill context selection. The permission picker is now protected. The diff-review selector is currently protected indirectly because the focused diff buffer exits insert mode before its normal-mode actions run.

## Scope

- Normalize mode at the narrowest shared LouiseLM selection boundary immediately before opening every vim.ui.select picker.
- Cover both stages of the session-options flow, especially the model/value picker opened by :LouiselmSessionOptions and the automatic picker scheduled by Chat:attach.
- Migrate or audit every raw vim.ui.select call in lua/louiselm/ui so no insert-mode-sensitive sibling remains.
- Preserve provider ownership of picker layout and interaction; do not detect or configure Snacks or another provider.
- Preserve selection values, cancellation behavior, asynchronous scheduling, and disposal guards.

## Acceptance Criteria

1. The automatically opened session-options overview is invoked outside insert mode after Chat:attach starts the prompt in insert mode.
2. The nested model/boolean value picker is also invoked outside insert mode.
3. Every LouiseLM vim.ui.select call either uses the shared normalization boundary or has a tested invariant proving insert mode cannot reach it.
4. The existing permission-picker mode regression remains green, and diff review remains in normal mode.
5. Headless behavioral tests cover the session-options regression and at least one representative shared/public or asynchronous selector path without relying on provider internals.
6. The focused UI tests, full MiniTest suite, StyLua check, and lua-language-server check pass.
close_reason: Normalized all 12 vim.ui.select call sites through one normal-mode picker boundary. Added red-green regressions for automatic/nested session options and file context selection. Verification: focused chat 44/44, context 5/5, diff 5/5; full MiniTest 185/185; StyLua and LuaLS passed; git diff --check passed.

title: Keep the chat header compact instead of dumping session metadata
description:
## Problem

The chat buffer header expands into a long Markdown heading containing every session option and context field. At normal split widths it wraps across visual rows, dominates the top of the conversation, and is difficult to scan.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Open a chat session whose agent reports several configuration options plus context or cost telemetry.
2. Display the chat in a typical narrow vertical split.
3. Observe that the level-one Markdown heading includes all metadata and wraps across multiple visual rows.

## Observed

A Codex session currently renders a heading such as:

`# codex · session-1 · ready · Mode=agent-full-access · Collaboration mode=default · Model=gpt-5.6-sol · Reasoning effort=xhigh · Fast mode=off · context=62585/258400 (24% normal) · Your turn`

The screenshot `/home/lotso/Pictures/scrot/20260809_0534_1920x1200_1786246460.png` shows this heading wrapping in the chat split.

## Expected

The transcript heading remains a compact, stable summary of session identity and current turn state, for example `# codex · session-1 · ready · Your turn`. Detailed configuration and telemetry remain discoverable through session options or a separate secondary status surface instead of being concatenated into an unbounded Markdown heading.

## Likely Root Cause

`session_summary()` appends every `config_options` entry plus context and cost telemetry, and `session_header()` uses the complete summary as the level-one Markdown heading. The heading length therefore scales with agent capabilities and enabled metadata.

## Acceptance Criteria

1. The level-one chat heading contains only concise session identity/lifecycle/turn information and stays readable at a typical vertical split width.
2. Static/default fields such as mode, collaboration mode, model, reasoning effort, and fast mode are not dumped into the transcript heading.
3. Detailed configuration remains accessible through the existing session-options flow or another clearly defined secondary surface; do not silently remove the ability to inspect or change supported options.
4. Useful dynamic telemetry such as context pressure or cost, if retained in the UI, is presented outside the primary Markdown heading and does not make that heading grow without bound.
5. Header updates for state changes, renamed sessions, loaded sessions, and turn transitions continue to work.
6. Add or update headless UI behavior tests using a session with several config options and context telemetry. Assert the compact buffer heading and continued access to configuration; use a manual narrow-split smoke check for wrapping rather than a pixel assertion.

## Scope

- In scope: chat header/status presentation and its behavioral tests.
- Out of scope: changing ACP session metadata, removing configuration controls, or redesigning the rest of the transcript.
close_reason: Split compact session identity from the detailed switcher summary so chat headings contain only name/agent/id/lifecycle/turn while options and telemetry remain accessible. Verification: focused chat suite 27/27 passed; full mini.test suite 112/112 passed; stylua --check . passed; lua-language-server reported zero diagnostics; 48-column headless smoke passed; git diff --check passed.

title: LouiselmToMarkdown prompts for a path before validating an explicit session id
description:
`:LouiselmToMarkdown <session_id>` prompts for a destination path before
checking whether `<session_id>` is actually attached, so an invalid id wastes
a full path-entry interaction before failing.

## Observed

Manual QA round on commits 674939b/4e4a58b, case 2.4 in QA_REVIEW.md. User
ran `:LouiselmToMarkdown not-a-session-id`, was shown the
"louiselm markdown path (blank for default):" prompt, typed a path, and only
then got the `louiselm: session is not attached` error. Expected (and every
other id-consuming failure in this command family gives) an immediate error
with no interactive prompt in between.

## Symptoms

- User types and confirms a file path for an export that was never going to
  happen.
- No data loss or crash — the eventual error message is correct — but the
  ordering is surprising and wastes an interaction.

## Root cause

`lua/louiselm/ui/chat/command.lua:266-282`:

```lua
nvim.api.nvim_create_user_command("LouiselmToMarkdown", function(arguments)
  ...
  local session_id = arguments.args ~= "" and arguments.args or nil
  nvim.ui.input({ prompt = "louiselm markdown path (blank for default): " }, function(path)
    ...
    local written_path, write_error = chat:to_markdown(session_id, path ~= "" and path or nil)
    ...
```

The session-id validity check lives inside `Chat:to_markdown`
(`init.lua:1553-1557`), which only runs after `vim.ui.input`'s callback
fires. `command.lua` has no way to check `session_id` validity up front
without reaching into `Chat`'s private `self.views` table.

## Why it was not caught

`tests/ui/chat_to_markdown_spec.lua` covers "not attached" at the
`Chat:to_markdown` level directly (bypassing the command layer), and
`tests/ui/command_spec.lua` stubs `vim.ui.input` so it never observes prompt
ordering relative to session validation. No test exercises the command's
real `vim.ui.input` flow with a bad session id end to end.

## Fix direction

Add a small public predicate, e.g. `Chat:is_attached(session_id)` (mirroring
the existing inline check in `Chat:switch`, init.lua:1444-1461), and have
`LouiselmToMarkdown` call it before opening the `vim.ui.input` prompt when an
explicit session id was given, reporting the error immediately instead.

Deliberately not fixing in the same pass as louiselm-dim, to keep that fix's
batch to the one crash bug; this is UX ordering, not a crash.

## Acceptance

- A test (likely in tests/ui/command_spec.lua, alongside its existing
  `vim.ui.input` stub) asserting that `:LouiselmToMarkdown <bad-id>` reports
  "session is not attached" without ever invoking the input prompt.
- Manually confirmed: `:LouiselmToMarkdown not-a-session-id` shows the error
  immediately, no path prompt.

## Not covered

Whether other future id-taking commands should share this predicate — only
`LouiselmToMarkdown` takes a raw typed session id today.

title: Write the example workflow document under docs/
description:
Write the maintainer's own workflow loop as an explicitly non-binding example document, at a `docs/` path.

This is the loop actually run today: **grill-me** (an idea gets direct attention and is interrogated one question at a time) → **to-beads** (the agreed plan becomes beads work items at the right abstraction level) → **sessions** (tasks get executed, automated or not) → **qa-review** (the maintainer manually tests what was just committed, and a defect found routes to `to-beads-bug`).

## Why this document exists

Two reasons, and both matter:

1. Other people, and other agents, may invent entirely different loops. Writing this one down as an *example* rather than a rule is what makes that possible without it reading as deviation from a contract.
2. louiselm intends to eventually ship this loop as an example **workflow config** — the maintainer's standing goal is that their workflow becomes expressible as configuration rather than convention. This document is the first draft of that spec. When the workflow-engine issues are picked up, this is what they implement against, rather than the loop being reconstructed from memory.

## What to write

Descriptive voice, not imperative — this describes what one person does, it does not instruct the reader. It must self-identify as a non-binding example in its opening, because the reader may arrive here without having read the link text in `AGENTS.md`.

Cover: what triggers each stage, what each stage hands to the next, and what "skill chaining" means here (one skill's output is designed to trigger another — grill-me ends by invoking to-beads; a qa-review defect invokes to-beads-bug).

Be honest about the known gap: a qa-review round can surface a *process* finding rather than a code bug, and there is currently no formalized route for that. It survives only by the maintainer noticing and calling for a grill-me session.

## Placement

A `docs/` path, not repo root. A root-level uppercase filename reads as law regardless of any disclaimer inside it, and that misreading is the specific thing this document must avoid. Do not create additional structure under `docs/` beyond what this one file needs.

## Acceptance criteria

- The document exists under `docs/` and declares itself a non-binding example within its opening lines.
- Each stage of the loop is described with its trigger and its handoff to the next stage.
- The unresolved process-finding gap is stated rather than papered over.
- It is written so that a future workflow-config implementation could use it as a starting spec, without committing to a config schema that does not exist yet.
- Voice is descriptive throughout; it never instructs the reader to adopt the loop.
close_reason: AGENTS.md section 2 added (sections renumbered 3-12), CLAUDE.md pointer added, docs/example-workflow.md written, triage requirement commented onto qbr.3/qbr.5, all seven memory notes migrated to repo or user-level instructions

title: Codex edit permissions are answered with a -32602 protocol error
description:
codex-acp sends edit permission requests with no reviewable payload at all:

title: Malformed ACP file-edit permission request terminates session
description:
## Reproduction

In session codex/019ff53a-629d-71a3-a1de-1a2506b42912, the agent sent an ACP session/request_permission file-edit request without a non-empty path. louiselm reported:

`Error: invalid ACP permission request: permission file edit must have a non-empty path`

The invalid request currently calls the session fatal-error path, closes the ACP client, and prevents the grilling session from continuing.

## Expected

Reject only the malformed permission request with a JSON-RPC invalid-params error. Keep the ACP session alive so the agent can continue or retry with a valid request.

## Acceptance criteria

- A file-edit permission request with a missing or empty path receives an error response with code -32602 and the validation message.
- The session remains ready/waiting for subsequent work and does not emit a fatal session error.
- Existing valid permission requests and malformed fatal startup/update handling remain unchanged.
- Add deterministic regression coverage.

title: Grill-me needed: how should qa-review rounds be archived, and does beads belong in the loop
description:
Not actionable as-is — this is a seed for a future grill-me session, not a
spec to implement from. Surfaced at the close of the transcript-export/
blog-publishing QA round (2026-08-18), when a process question came up that
didn't fit anywhere in the existing skill chain.

## The open questions

- **Archiving authority.** Once a qa-review round closes, does the working
  file (`QA_REVIEW.md`-style) become the durable record of what was tested
  and found, or is it disposable scratch once findings are filed to beads?
  Right now nothing says either way, so rounds just accumulate as loose
  untracked files.
- **Where archiving sits in the qa-review process.** Should the qa-review
  skill itself have a defined "closing" step that decides what happens to
  the file (commit it, summarize it into beads, delete it), or is that
  always a manual call by whoever's running the round?
- **Could beads be leveraged more directly.** Instead of (or alongside) a
  markdown working file, could a qa-review round's cases/results live in
  beads itself — e.g. as a parent issue with the plan, sub-issues per case?
  Unclear if that's better or just adds ceremony to something that works
  fine as a file today.

## Why this doesn't fit the usual chain

Their standing workflow is grill-me -> to-beads -> tasks executed across
sessions ("skill chaining"). Within a qa-review round, a code bug correctly
triggers to-beads-bug — that chain already works. But this round produced a
different kind of finding: not a bug, a question about the skills/workflow
itself. There's currently no formalized way for a skill to route that kind
of self-reflective finding anywhere — it only survived this time because the
user happened to notice and say it was worth a grill-me session. Whether
findings like this should sometimes get folded directly into a skill's own
instructions (when concrete enough) versus always deferred to a grill-me
session (when still vague) is itself part of what's open here.

## A concrete proposal already on record

This question isn't new — the user raised it explicitly at the *start* of
this same QA round, in an earlier session (`claude/85f97534-8fa6-4d95-a05a-7c0851bec937`):
"while we do this i want you to think if those reviews conversation or
document you produce as part of the review could leverage beads for
historical / archiving purposes." That session's assistant answered with a
concrete sketch the user liked and wants preserved verbatim here for the
grill-me session to react to, not re-derive:

1. **One bead per round**, type `chore`, label `qa-round`, created with
   `--description-file QA_REVIEW.md`. The whole plan lands in
   `.beads/issues.jsonl`, which is committed — so the round becomes
   greppable history instead of an untracked file you have to decide about
   at the end. That's the exact question that ended the *previous* round
   (the permissions round) unresolved too: "commit it as a record, or
   delete it."
2. **Findings hang off it as children.** `br create -t bug --parent
   <round-id>` — the graph then answers "which round found this?" and `br
   graph` shows a round's blast radius. This round's findings
   (`louiselm-dim`, `louiselm-euj`, `louiselm-d2o`, `louiselm-xrf`) are
   already beads but orphaned from the round that produced them — exactly
   the gap this proposal closes.
3. **Round-by-round narration goes in `br comments add`** — append-only and
   timestamped, matching the loop shape (plan, run, learn, edit). The
   markdown file stays the live scratchpad *during* the round since it
   churns every round; beads takes the final state on close.
4. **`--external-ref` holds the session id** (e.g.
   `claude/21a0ede3-b65e-4f1c-935d-754f22126384` for this round), which
   dovetails with the user's global commit-message rule (`Refs <id>` for
   named sessions/issues), and `br orphans` catches anything referenced in a
   commit but still open.

The convergence the prior session flagged as the nice part: the
transcript-export feature this very round was testing turns a session into
a publishable artifact. So under this proposal the bead becomes the index,
the exported transcript is the evidence, and a blog post (via the same
publishing pipeline, once `louiselm-xrf` is fixed) is the human-readable
version of the same round — three layers of the same feature set reused for
QA's own record-keeping instead of a fourth bespoke mechanism.

## Bigger context

Connects to a broader, previously-discussed wish: the user's own workflow
(grill-me/beads/session-chaining) eventually being expressible as a
configurable part of louiselm itself, not just a convention they follow by
hand. Not fully re-litigated here — worth pulling that thread in the
grill-me session too.

## Not covered

No decision on the concrete proposal above — it was well-received when
sketched, but never evaluated against the three open questions or actually
tried on a round (this round still used a plain `QA_REVIEW.md`). Left for
the grill-me session: whether to adopt it as-is, adapt it, or reject it in
favor of something else.
close_reason: Resolved via grill-me. Routed to feature louiselm-ri1 (Give qa-review rounds a mandatory archiving/closing step backed by beads), with child tasks louiselm-ri1.1 (skill closing step) and louiselm-ri1.2 (retroactive close of QA_REVIEW.md and QA_REVIEW-permissions-round.md, blocked on ri1.1). Adopted the concrete proposal on record as-is: one chore/qa-round bead per round via --description-file + --external-ref, findings as children via the existing to-beads-bug chain, cases stay flat (never beaded), narration via br comments, working file deleted on close. Bigger workflow-config-engine thread explicitly left out of scope per agreement.
